title: Sell Mineral Rights in Jacksonburg, WV
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Jacksonburg, WV
metaDescription: Jacksonburg, Wetzel County mineral owners: core Marcellus acreage, legacy family farm tracts, and title work through the Wetzel County Courthouse.
heroLead: Jacksonburg sits in Wetzel County's core Marcellus ground, where family farm tracts and modern horizontal units now overlap on the same acreage.
intro: Wetzel County is widely considered part of the thickest, most productive stretch of the Marcellus fairway in West Virginia, and Jacksonburg's surrounding farmland has seen its share of horizontal permitting as a result. Many tracts here were originally leased under older farm-family agreements before being pooled into larger modern units.

sections.heading: Farm-tract ownership meets modern unit development
paragraphs: Jacksonburg-area acreage has historically been held in family farm tracts, some passed down through direct inheritance and some split among multiple heirs as generations pass. When an operator pools several of these tracts into a horizontal spacing unit, each owner's royalty becomes a pro-rata share of the unit rather than tied to a single well the way older vertical leases worked.

sections.heading: Confirming your lease and royalty terms
paragraphs: Because Wetzel County has seen multiple leasing waves over the past two decades, it's common for a Jacksonburg tract to carry a lease that was assigned from one operator to another, sometimes more than once. Confirming which lease currently governs your interest — and whether the royalty rate reflects modern terms or an older, lower percentage — starts with a records check at the Wetzel County Courthouse in New Martinsville.

sections.heading: Pipeline and gathering-line easements on the same tracts
paragraphs: Wetzel County's drilling density means a lot of Jacksonburg-area acreage also carries gathering-line or pipeline right-of-way agreements layered on top of the mineral lease, negotiated separately and sometimes with a different company than the one operating the wellbore. These easements don't change your mineral ownership, but they're worth identifying since they show up in the same courthouse chain and occasionally affect surface access disputes tied to a mineral sale.

If you're weighing a sale, a buyer will typically want to see both the lease and any recorded easements affecting the tract, since together they establish the full picture of what's encumbering the acreage beyond the mineral interest itself.

faqs.question: Is Jacksonburg considered core Marcellus territory?
faqs.answer: Yes, Wetzel County overall is regarded as some of the thickest, most active Marcellus acreage in the state, and Jacksonburg's surrounding tracts have seen corresponding horizontal development.

faqs.question: My lease has been assigned between operators more than once — does that affect my royalty?
faqs.answer: The royalty percentage set in your original lease generally carries forward through an assignment, but it's worth confirming the current operator of record and reviewing your division orders to make sure payments match your lease terms.

faqs.question: How do I find out which unit my Jacksonburg tract falls in?
faqs.answer: Request the unit plat from your operator or have a courthouse records check run cross-referencing your deed against filed pooling orders.

faqs.question: Does a pipeline easement on my tract reduce my mineral interest's value?
faqs.answer: Generally no — an easement affects surface use, not mineral ownership, though a buyer will want to see it recorded as part of a full title picture.
